title: Evals in practice: building a test set that survives contact
summary: How to build an evaluation set for your own AI system that keeps telling the truth after it meets users, graders and the model itself: cases drawn from real failures, labels two experts would agree on, judges with their own held-out sets, error bars and sample size, contamination, broken harnesses, and why teams distrust their own dashboards.

topics: deep dive: evals in practice — building a test set that survives contact
concepts_taught: building a product eval set that survives contact: start from 20-50 real failures and error analysis (open then axial coding to saturation), structured synthetic cases by dimension, balanced should/shouldn't cases, and capability evals that start low and graduate into near-100% regression suites

labels and graders as the weak link: criteria drift, a principal domain expert giving binary pass/fail plus critique, two-experts-agree as the task test, LLM judges validated on a held-out split with true-positive and true-negative rates rather than raw agreement, and label errors that can flip model rankings

eval statistics and contamination in practice: standard errors, clustered errors for grouped questions, paired comparisons, roughly a thousand questions to detect a three-point difference; fresh matched sets (GSM1k, ImageNet v2) as the contamination test; broken graders and leaky environments (CORE-Bench, shared git history) as the commonest false signal
